 (a) Every agenda for regular meetings shall provide an opportunity for members of the
 public to directly address the legislative body on any item of interest to the public, before

 jurisdiction of the legislative body, provided that no action shall be taken on any item not

City Council  Wednesday, January 10, 2024
  Section 54954.2 [section omitted].

 (b) (1) The legislative body of a local agency may adopt reasonable regulations to ensure
 that the intent of the subdivision (a) is carried out, including, but not limited to, regulations
 limiting the total amount of time allocated for public testimony on particular issues and for
 each individual speaker.
  (2) Notwithstanding paragraph (1), when the legislative body of a local agency limits
 time for public comment, the legislative body of a local agency shall provide at least twice
 the allotted time to a member of the public who utilizes a translator to ensure that non-
 English speakers receive the same opportunity to directly address the legislative body of
 a local agency.”

 In furtherance of Section 54954.3 of the Brown Act, the public is allotted to speak a total
 of two (2) minutes on the entirety of the Consent Calendar, Appointment(s), New
 Business and Closed Session, with two (2) minutes on each Public Hearing, and, if
 desired, an additional two (2) minutes on items not on the agenda that are within the
 subject matter jurisdiction of the City Council. As specified in the Brown Act, a speaker
 utilizing a translator will receive twice the amount of time specified.

SUBJECT:  RECEIVE AND FILE THE MONTHLY INVESTMENT ACTIVITY
  REPORT FOR NOVEMBER 2023

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council receive and file the monthly investment activity
report for the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency for November 2023.
BACKGROUND
Pursuant to Section 16 of the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency Investment
Policy, the City Treasurer shall prepare and present monthly and quarterly reports on
investments to the City Manager/Executive Director and the City Council/Directors. The
reports shall detail the type of investment, name of the issuer, purchase date, date of
maturity, amount of deposit, and rate of interest. This information shall be provided for
all City and Successor Agency pooled investments, as well as for Certificates of
Participation, Revenue Bonds, Tax Allocation Bonds, Assessment Districts, and
Community Facilities District accounts, which are managed by outside Fiscal Agents.

The monthly investment reports provide a synopsis of the investment activity for the City
of Palmdale and Successor Agency. The reports provide information on assets,
allocations, average maturities, yields, and book valuations. The interest rates
presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this report.

The market values presented for pooled City and Successor Agency investments are
based on closing prices for the related investment as of the date of this report. This
information was obtained from the Wall Street Journal, Bloomberg Financial Markets,
Capital Market Finances, or other reliable sources of market prices.
DISCUSSION
Compliance with Investment Policy

For November, the invested portfolio amount for the City of Palmdale totaled
$306,128,068, a decrease of $4,933,057 from the previous month, and an increase of
$20,487,809 in comparison to last year. The monthly decrease is primarily the result of
a withdrawal from LAIF during the month to cover debt service and operating expenses.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Monthly Investment Reports
January 10, 2024
Page 2

The par value of Successor Agency’s portfolio as of November was $7,955,102. The
balance increased by $6,102 from last month due to earned interest during the month.

All investments meet criteria appropriate to Section 8 of the Investment Policy. The
portfolios are based on a combination of various investments, including CDs, Corporate
Notes, U.S. Treasury Securities, and Government Agency Paper, each adhering to
portfolio percentage limitations.

The Finance Division is the custodian for the City and Successor Agency’s investment
portfolio and follows the three main principles of both entities’ investment policies to 1)
Investment in financial instruments that mitigate the risk of monetary losses stemming
from market fluctuations; 2) Establish and maintain a portfolio that has sufficient liquidity
to allow the City and Successor Agency to meet all anticipated cash requirements; and
3) Seek out investment instruments that provide a competitive market rate of return.

Liquidity

One core approach the Finance Division focuses on is providing liquidity to measure up
to the City and Successor Agency’s operational requirements. Thus, the Finance
Division is currently investing in two pooled funds, Local Agency Investment Fund (LAIF)
and California Asset Management Program (CAMP). These are intended for daily
operational activities and used for economic uncertainties and maintenance needs. The
pooled funds provide a higher liquidity ratio to ensure the City and Successor Agency
meet cash flow requirements.

The total LAIF balance for the City of Palmdale at the end of November is $128,703,931.
The decrease of $5,000,000 from the prior month is due to a withdrawal to general fund
for the payment of debt service and other operating expenses.

Successor Agency LAIF balance at the end of November was $6,215,832. A decrease
of $900,000 from the prior month was due to debt service payments made during the
month.

CAMP’s balance for City of Palmdale at the end of November was $265,347 compared
to October balance of $264,136. The slight increase is due to interest earned during the
month.

The interest rates presented are the most current rates available as of the date of this
report. As of November 30, 2023, the interest rates for LAIF and CAMP investments
were at 3.843 percent and 5.58 percent, respectively. By comparison, the LAIF and
CAMP interest rates at the end of October were at 3.670 percent and 5.56 percent. Both
rates have slightly increased within this month. This time last year, LAIF and CAMP
rates were at 2.007 percent and 3.90, respectively.

The chart above shows both the Local Agency Investment Fund and California Asset
Management Program’s average monthly yields beginning February 2023 through
November 2023.

We anticipate that rates will remain consistent, with only minor variations in the
upcoming months. The difference between the performance of the two funds is partly
due to the varying pool characteristics. CAMP's portfolio composition is much more
prone to market volatility, resulting in performance variations.

Diversity
The Finance Division aims to diversify the investment portfolios to avoid incurring
unreasonable and avoidable risks regarding specific security types or individual financial
institutions.

The City of Palmdale and Successor Agency’s investment portfolios remain strongly
diversified. The monthly report includes all investments held by both entities and current
book values as of November 30, 2023.

It is anticipated that both the City of Palmdale and Successor Agency will have sufficient
sums of money to meet their expenditure requirements for the next six months. The
Finance Division will continue to monitor current economic conditions and the impact on
interest rates.

Attached are summaries of the investments in the City of Palmdale and Successor
Agency’s books as of November 30, 2023.

SUBJECT:  ADOPT RESOLUTION CC 2024-003 AMENDING THE
  HUMAN RESOURCES RULES AND REGULATIONS

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution CC 2024-003 amending the Human Resources Rules and
  Regulations.

BACKGROUND
Currently, unbenefited part-time employees receive 28 hours of paid sick leave per fiscal
year, based on California State Law. 28 hours of sick leave is made available to
employees on the first day of employment, or on the first day of the fiscal year. Unused
sick time at the end of each fiscal year is forfeited.

DISCUSSION
To comply with new California state law, effective January 1, 2024, unbenefited
employees will now receive 40 hours of sick leave per year. It will be based on a calendar
year instead of a fiscal year as it was previously. Any unused sick hours in the employee’s
accrued leave sick banks as of December 31, 2023, will be lost, and the full 40 hours for
2024 will be loaded into part-time employee sick leave banks. Unused hours do not roll
over to the next calendar year.

In accordance with Senate Bill 616, there is a 90-day waiting period before new hires may
use sick leave. This waiting period remains in effect.

FISCAL IMPACT
The fiscal impact may vary depending on the number of part-time staff, hourly rates, and
sick time usage. The maximum fiscal impact to the City in Fiscal Year 2023-24 is
$108,000.

Section 10-3 Sick Leave (Rev. 01/2024)

  Paid sick leave shall not be considered a right which an employee may use at his
or her discretion. Sick leave shall be used by employees for the following: (1) Diagnosis,
care, or treatment of an existing health condition of, or preventive care for, an employee
or an employee’s family member; or (2) For an employee who is a victim of domestic
violence, sexual assault, or stalking. Family members include the employee’s parent,
child, spouse, registered domestic partner, grandparent, grandchild, sibling or
designated person.
  When the need for sick leave is foreseeable, an employee must personally give
the employee's supervisor as much advance notice as possible of the need to take sick
leave. When the need for sick leave is not foreseeable, and except as otherwise
required by law, an employee must personally give the employee's supervisor notice of
the need to take sick leave as soon as practical. When possible, such notice shall be
given before the start of the employee's scheduled workday and prior to the start of
each additional workday thereafter that the employee is absent. If it is impossible for the
employee to notify his or her supervisor, the employee must notify his or her department
head. In addition, all absences shall be reported in accordance with departmental rules.
  Eligible employees earn paid sick leave based on hours worked or hours paid
(e.g., when an employee is on paid leave). Full-time employees earn sick leave at the
rate of eight (8) hours per month. Benefited part-time employees earn sick leave on a
prorated basis. Paid sick leave is not earned (i.e., does not accrue) during unpaid
leaves of absence, except as otherwise required by state or federal law.
  Full-time and benefited part-time employees hired on or before August 1, 2012
may accumulate sick leave without a limit. Individuals who become full-time employees
on or after August 2, 2012 may accumulate a maximum of 800 hours of sick leave.
Individuals who became benefited part-time employees on or after August 2, 2012 may
accumulate a maximum of 400 hours of sick leave.
  Unbenefited, Seasonal and Variable Hour Employees shall receive forty (40)
hours of paid sick leave on January 1st for use during that calendar year. Newly hired
Unbenefited, Seasonal and Variable Hour Employees shall receive forty (40) hours of
sick leave on their first day of employment. An Unbenefited, Seasonal or Variable Hour
Employee may use accrued sick leave beginning on the 90th day of employment.
Unused sick hours do not carry over to the next calendar year.
  Full-time and benefited part-time employees are not eligible to use sick leave
until it has been accrued. Sick leave may only be used in increments of fifteen minutes
unless smaller increments are permitted by law. Sick leave must be reported on
appropriate forms.
  Retaliation or discrimination against an employee who uses paid sick leave is
prohibited by City policy and California state law.
  An employee who returns to work for the City within one year of separation of
service will be credited with up to forty (40) hours of sick leave. If the employee
separated with less than forty (40) hours of accrued sick leave, then he/she will be
credited with the number of hours he/she had accrued at the time of separation.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-004, a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale designating by title and name those officials who are authorized to
  sign checks and warrants, and repeal Resolution No. CC 2023-074.
  2. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2024-011, a Resolution of the Successor Agency to the
  Community Redevelopment Agency of the City of Palmdale designating by title
  and name those officials who are authorized to sign checks and warrants, and
  repeal Resolution No. SA 2022-003.
BACKGROUND
The Palmdale Municipal Code (PMC) Section 3.14.030 requires that the City Council
designate by Resolution the names of those individuals holding offices identified in PMC
03.14.020 as authorized signers of checks, drafts, warrants, or other orders for payment
of money drawn in the name of the City and the Successor Agency.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the Successor Agency to the Community Redevelopment
Agency of the City of Palmdale:

  1. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2024-009 approving the Administrative Budget for the
  Period of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 (Administrative Budget 24-25).
  2. Adopt Resolution No. SA 2024-010 approving the Recognized Obligation
  Payment Schedule (ROPS 24-25) for the period of July 1, 2024 through June 30,
  2025.

BACKGROUND
Assembly Bill 1X 26 (AB 26) was signed by the Governor on June 28, 2011 and upheld
as constitutional by the California Supreme Court. On June 27, 2012, the Governor
signed Assembly Bill 1484 (AB 1484). AB 26 and AB 1484 (together the Dissolution
Bills) made sweeping changes to California Redevelopment Law, eliminating
redevelopment agencies statewide, establishing successor agencies, and requiring the
successor agencies to pay, perform, and enforce the enforceable obligations of the
former redevelopment agencies and to wind down the affairs of the former
redevelopment agencies.

Administrative Budget

Section 34177(j) of the Dissolution Bills requires the Successor Agency to prepare an
Administrative Budget annually and submit it to the Los Angeles County Fifth
Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval.

Section 34177(k) of the Dissolution Bills further requires the Successor Agency to
provide the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller the administrative cost estimates
from its approved Administrative Budget that are to be paid from property tax revenues
deposited in the Redevelopment Property Tax Trust Fund.

Health & Safety Code Section 34171(b)(3) states that commencing July 1, 2016, the
administrative cost allowance shall be up to 3 percent of the actual property tax
distributed to the successor agency by the county auditor-controller in the preceding
fiscal year for payment of approved enforceable obligations, reduced by the successor
agency’s administrative cost allowance and loan repayments made to the city pursuant
to Section 34191.4(b) during the preceding fiscal year, subject to a minimum of
$250,000, unless such amount is reduced by the Oversight Board or by agreement
between the successor agency and the State Department of Finance (“Department of
Finance”). Staff has estimated this amount and allocated it to various Successor Agency
costs as detailed in Exhibit A to Resolution No. SA 2024-009.

Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS)

Section 34177(l) of the Dissolution Bills requires the Successor Agency to prepare a
Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS) listing the enforceable obligations of
the former Redevelopment Agency on an annual basis.

Section 34177(l) further requires that (i) the ROPS shall be submitted to the county
administrative officer, the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller (Auditor-Controller)
and the State Department of Finance (Department of Finance) at the same time that the
Successor Agency submits the ROPS to the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial
District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval; (ii) the ROPS shall be submitted to
and duly approved by the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated
Oversight Board; (iii) the approved ROPS shall be posted on the Successor Agency’s
website; and (iv) the approved ROPS shall be submitted to the Auditor-Controller, the
State Controller and the State Department of Finance.

Section 34180 of the Dissolution Bills (Section 34180) requires certain successor
agency actions to be approved by the oversight board, including Section 34180(c)
“Setting aside of amounts in reserves as required by indentures, trust indentures, or
similar documents governing the issuance of outstanding redevelopment agency
bonds.” The attached ROPS 24-25 details amounts in accordance with Section
34180(c).

The attached ROPS 24-25 also includes an enforceable obligation for the repayment of
the Educational Revenue Augmentation Fund (“ERAF”) and Supplemental Educational
Revenue Augmentation Fund (“SERAF”) loans borrowed from the former
Redevelopment Agency’s Low and Moderate Income Housing Fund.

Senate Bill No. 107 (section 14 of Chapter 325, Statutes of 2015) states that the
Successor Agency’s Oversight Board continues to exist and will only cease to exist after
all of its indebtedness has been repaid, and thus, requires that the City’s Successor
Agency’s Oversight Board approve ROPS 24-25.

DISCUSSION
The attached Resolution Nos. SA 2024-009 and SA 2024-010 seek approval of the
Administrative Budget 24-25 and the Recognized Obligation Payment Schedule (ROPS)
24-25.

Approval of the Administrative Budget and the ROPS will allow the City to remain in
compliance with AB 26 and AB 1484 (together the Dissolution Bills), and to submit the
information timely to the county administrative officer, the Los Angeles County Auditor-
Controller (Auditor-Controller) and the State Department of Finance (Department of
Finance). Simultaneously, the Successor Agency submits the ROPS to the Los Angeles
County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated Oversight Board for approval.

Upon approval from the Los Angeles County Fifth Supervisorial District Consolidated
Oversight Board, and the State Department of Finance, the City may then incorporate the
requested administrative budgets and payments from the ROPS in the City’s annual
budget for Fiscal Year 2024-25.

FISCAL IMPACT
The Administrative Budget for the period of July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2025 totals
$311,025. These funds will be included in various line items in Program 20 of Fund 460
in the fiscal year 2024-25 budget and are included on the Recognized Obligation Payment
Schedule (ROPS). These funds will be used to reimburse the City for its staff hours.

The total payments estimated during the one-year period of ROPS 24-25 is $16,508,320,
of which $11,077,908 is expected to be funded by Redevelopment Property Tax Trust
Funds (RPTTF) to be received from the Los Angeles County Auditor-Controller (including
Administrative Cost Allowance), $5,417,401 is from reserve balance funds, and $13,011
is from other funds. Amounts are to be budgeted in various areas of the Successor
Agency and Housing Successor Agency budgets.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Approve Law Enforcement Feasibility Study Agreement No. A-8630 with Citygate
  Associates, LLC in the amount of $178,453 for a term of six (6) months; and
  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to execute the Agreement No. A-
  8630 with Citygate Associates, LLC, including non-substantive changes.

BACKGROUND
For the past 61 years, the City of Palmdale (City) has contracted with Los Angeles
County to provide its law enforcement through the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s
Department (LASD). The City’s population has grown 6% from 2013 to its current
population of 165,917. The cost of providing law enforcement services has increased
58% from 2013. The current fiscal year cost for service and the Liability Trust Fund is
$31,812,605. Looking forward, the City is concerned the annual increase in the cost to
contract with LASD will be cost prohibitive and alternative approaches for providing
public safety services should be explored and discussed. In the past ten years, the City
has been successful in reducing its per 10,000 population Part I Crime Rate incidents
from the upper 300 range to below 200 range through strong collaboration with the Los
Angeles County Sheriff’s Palmdale Station and innovative community programs. These
efforts include monthly meetings with the Station Captain and specialized teams, a
robust single and multi-family Neighborhood Watch program, providing strong outreach
and education to the community, engagement with community partners, collaboration
with the Code Enforcement Division, and providing Community Service Officers. In
addition to the increasing cost of public safety the City is concerned with the level of
customer service, the increasing shortage of sworn personnel and the LASD response
times to non-emergency calls.

DISCUSSION
The City released Request for Proposal (RFP) No. 23-001-2500 for the Law
Enforcement Feasibility Study August 17, 2023. The Scope of Services is for a qualified
 Report to Mayor and City Council

firm to analyze the current service levels of the City’s public safety services and
programs to determine if its current model is sustainable, if modification of Palmdale’s
current strategies and programs should be considered and additional approaches for
the City to consider. All options should be explored, and include associated costs, cost
savings and potential liabilities.
The preferred vendor must have at least five years of experience in the areas of law
enforcement, operations, public safety programming, community outreach and
engagement, and the ability to present innovative strategies and concepts for the City
to review in its effort to provide effective and sustainable service levels to the community
and its residents.
PlanetBids, the City’s online bid system, notified 267 City of Palmdale vendors and
considered 20 of these to be perspective bidders. Proposals were received from five
firms, Berry Dunn (Portland, Maine), Citygate Associates, LLC (Folsom, California),
Jensen Hughes (Chicago, Illinois), Matrix Consulting Group (San Mateo, California), and
The Consortium of Rothschild/Lawrence (Wilmington, Delaware). Evaluation criteria
included past performance and experience, reference responses, qualifications and
abilities of the proposer’s team, project timeline and milestones, cost, the technical
proposed plan, overall quality and presentation of the proposer’s response documents,
and interviews. The evaluation team selected Citygate Associates, LLC to provide the
Law Enforcement Feasibility Study.

  CONTRACT FOR CONSULTANT SERVICES
  BETWEEN THE CITY OF PALMDALE AND CITYGATE ASSOCIATES, LLC

THIS CONTRACT FOR CONSULTANT SERVICES (“Contract” herein) is made and
entered into by and between the City of Palmdale a public body corporate and politic,
(hereinafter called “CITY”) and CITYGATE ASSOCIATES, LLC (hereinafter called
“CONSULTANT”). This Contract shall become effective on the date of the last
signatory.

  RECITALS

  WHEREAS, City desires to engage CONSULTANT to provide certain
consultant services; and

  WHEREAS, CONSULTANT represents that CONSULTANT has the expertise
and is qualified to perform the services described in this Contract. And, if required, is
duly registered under the laws of the State of California; and

  WHEREAS, CONSULTANT desires to accept such engagement.

NOW, THEREFORE, the parties agree as follows:

1  DESCRIPTION OF WORK

1.1  The City hereby engages CONSULTANT, and CONSULTANT accepts such
engagement, to provide the following services:

Law Enforcement Feasibility Study providing analysis of:
The City’s police service needs;
Service levels provided by the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department (LASD);
Collaboration of the City’s innovative community programs, including engagement
with community partners;
Collaboration with the Public Safety Department.

Citygate’s Scope of Work will include:
Organizational Review;
Operational Review;
Findings and Recommendations.

Project deliverables include:
Kickoff Meeting;
Project Plan;
Bi-Weekly Check-ins;
City Council Briefing;
Midpoint Draft Report for review;
Final Report.

CONSULTANT shall perform and complete all such work and services in a manner
satisfactory to CITY.

1.2  Project deliverables shall be reviewed and approved by CITY to determine
acceptable completion. CITY shall have the right to review and inspect the work
during the course of its performance at such times as may be specified by CITY.

1.3  CONSULTANT shall not accept any change of scope, or change in contract
provisions, unless issued in writing, as a contract change order or amendment and
signed by CITY. Any extensions of time must be mutually agreed upon in writing and
executed by both parties.

1.4  CITY shall provide to CONSULTANT, without charge, all data, program
information, including reports, records, maps, and other information, now in CITY’s
possession, which may facilitate the timely performance of the work.

13 TERMINATION FOR CAUSE

13.1 If the City determines that the CONSULTANT has failed to supply an
adequate working force, or to provide services of proper quality, or has failed in any
other respect to satisfactorily perform the services specified in this Contract, the City
shall give written notice to the CONSULTANT specifying all defaults to be remedied
within thirty (30) days. Such notice shall set forth the basis for the City’s
dissatisfaction and suggest corrective measures. If, after thirty days, the
CONSULTANT has failed to implement the corrective measures, the City may elect to
terminate this Contract, in whole or in part.

13.2 In the event the City terminates this Contract in whole or in part as provided
herein above, the City may procure, upon such terms and in such manner, as it may
deem appropriate, services similar to those terminated.

13.3 If this Contract is terminated as provided above, the City may require the
CONSULTANT to provide all finished or unfinished documents, data, studies,
software, drawings, maps, photographs, reports, etc., prepared by the
CONSULTANT. Upon such termination, the CONSULTANT shall be paid an amount
equal to the value of the services provided and work performed as of the date of
termination. Such payment by the City may take into consideration the costs
associated with hiring another CONSULTANT to complete the services. In the event
no new CONSULTANT is employed, the CONSULTANT shall be paid an amount
equal to the value of the work performed. In ascertaining the value of the work
performed up to the date of termination, consideration shall be given to both
completed work and work in progress, to complete and incomplete documents when
such are delivered to CITY, and to authorized reimbursement expenses.

The above is in addition to any other remedies available by law or equity to the City.

13.4 If, after notice of termination of the Contract under the provisions of this
Section 13, it is determined, for any reason, that CONSULTANT was not in default, or
that the default was excusable, then the rights and obligations of the parties shall be
the same as if the notice of termination had been issued pursuant to Section 12.

 Section 1 - Purpose of the RFP
The purpose of this RFP is to solicit competitive proposals from a qualified firm or consultant (together
“Consultant”) for Law Enforcement Feasibility Study, in accordance with the attached specifications and
general terms and conditions.
City of Palmdale Background:
The City of Palmdale was incorporated on August 24, 1962. At incorporation, the City encompassed 2.1
square miles. Since that time numerous annexations and sphere of influence amendments have been
approved by the County’s Local Agency Formation Commission (LAFCO). Currently, the City covers 104.59
square miles. Palmdale is ideally located approximately 60 miles north of downtown Los Angeles in the
Antelope Valley within Los Angeles County. To the north it is bounded by unincorporated communities of
Lake Los Angeles and Littlerock, to the south it is bounded by unincorporated community of Acton and to
the west is bounded by the unincorporated community of Leona Valley.
Government Structure:
Palmdale is a Charter City governed under the City Council/City Manage form of local government. The City
Council consists of five members who serve four-year staggered terms, elected from the City by districts
with a rotating Mayor. As a legislative body, the City Council is responsible for the enactment of local laws
(Ordinances), the adoption of the annual City Budget and Capital Improvement Plan, and the review and
adoption of proposed policies, agreements, contracts, and other City business items. The City Manager is
responsible for directing the City’s operations and administrative processes, as well as, directing and
overseeing the implementation of policies crafted by the City Council.
City Structure:
The City of Palmdale currently provides general administrative, recreational, and library services, and
performs development processing and public works functions. Fire prevention and protection are provided
through the Los Angeles County Consolidated Fire Department. Police and animal control services are also
provided under contract by Los Angeles County.
Los Angeles County Sheriff Department Services:
For the past 61 years, the City of Palmdale (City), as a municipality and later as a charter city, has contracted
with Los Angeles County to provide its law enforcement through the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s
Department (LASD). The City population has grown from 126,645 in 2003 to 156,029 in 2013 to its current
population of 165,917 and so has the cost of providing law enforcement services. The current fiscal year cost
for service and the Liability Trust Fund is $31,812,605.80. Looking forward, the City is concerned the annual
increase in the cost to contract with LASD will be cost-prohibitive and alternative approaches to providing
public safety services need to be explored and discussed. In the past ten years, the City of Palmdale has
been successful in reducing its per 10,000 population Part I Crime Rate incidents from the upper 300 range
to the below 200 range through a strong collaboration with the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Palmdale
Station and innovative community programs. These efforts include monthly meetings with the Station
Captain and specialized teams, a robust single and multi-family Neighborhood Watch program, providing
strong outreach and education to the community, engagement with community partners, collaboration with
the Code Enforcement Division, and providing Community Service Officers. In addition to the increasing cost
of public safety the City is concerned with the level of customer service, the increasing shortage of sworn
personnel, and the LASD response times to non-emergency calls.

NOTE: (Section 3 Scope of Services/Work will be incorporated into the resulting contract).
Services shall include, but are not necessarily limited to the following:
The City is seeking through this Request for Proposals a qualified firm that can analyze the current service
levels of the City’s public safety services and City programs to determine if its current model is sustainable, if
modification of Palmdale’s current strategies and programs should be considered and additional strategies
the City should consider. The City will provide to the successful candidate information including an overview

statistics, and the City’s current programs and staffing including those listed above. All options should be

  1. Approve the Subrecipient Agreement (A-8658) with Antelope Valley Domestic
  Violence Council DBA Valley Oasis to administer the HOME Investments
  Partnerships Funded Tenant Based Rental Assistance Program in an amount not
  to exceed $787,500 for a term of four years and six months; and
  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to make necessary changes and
  execute documents related to the HOME Investments Partnerships Funded
  Tenant Based Rental Assistance Program.

DISCUSSION
On May 3, 2023, the City Council approved the 2023-2024 Action Plan approving the
HOME Investment Partnerships Grant funded (HOME) Tenant Based Rental Assistance
(TBRA) program. Since implementation in 2016, the TBRA program has annually assisted
up to 32 extremely low-income senior households with a severe cost burden of paying
more than 50% of their income on rent.

The City’s Consolidated Plan analysis has identified assistance to seniors 62 and above
as a high priority. Many senior households are on extremely low or fixed incomes and are
in critical need of assistance. Providing rental assistance to these households will allow
them to meet basic needs including food and prescription medication. The TBRA program
continues to be essential as monthly rents continue to rise.

On September 24, 2023, staff posted Request for Proposals (RFP) 23-002-6400 for the
Tenant Based Rental Assistance (TBRA) program on PlanetBids. Through PlanetBids,
53 vendors were notified of the RFP, and 16 were considered prospective. Of the 16

On October 27, 2023, staff reissued Request for Proposals (RFP) 23-006-6400 for the
Tenant Based Rental Assistance (TBRA) program on PlanetBids. Through PlanetBids,
54 vendors were notified of the RFP, and 16 were considered prospective. Of the 16

was received. No contact was received from other potential responders. The proposal
underwent an RFP evaluation process that included an individual and group evaluation.
The result of the evaluation process is the recommendation to award the contract to
Antelope Valley Domestic Violence Council DBA Valley Oasis.

Both bids were advertised through PlanetBids, the Antelope Valley Press, the City of
Palmdale website and sent to local organizations via email.

  SHELTER CRISIS IN THE CITY OF PALMDALE

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:
  1. Adopt Resolution No. CC 2024-008 a Resolution of the City Council of the City
  of Palmdale Declaring a Shelter Crisis in the City of Palmdale; and
  2. Authorize the City Manager or her designee to take all actions convenient and
  necessary during this period of shelter crisis.

BACKGROUND
The Antelope Valley Service Planning Area 1 (SPA 1) point-in-time count by the Los
Angeles Homeless Services Authority (LAHSA) was 4,598 in 2022 and 4,686 in 2023.
In 2022, the point-in-time count for Unhoused People in the City of Palmdale (City) was
309, including 61 living in shelters, 7 in transitional housing, 27 on the street, and 214
unsheltered, which included those living in vehicles, tents, RVs, and makeshift shelters.
In 2023, the point-in-time count for Unhoused People in the City was 515, comprised of
65 in shelters, 112 unsheltered, and 338 estimated living in vehicles, tents, RVs, and
makeshift shelters. The number of unsheltered persons between 2022 and 2023
increased by 124 or 57.94%.
Palmdale during 2023 experienced 58 days with temperatures of 32 degrees and below
and 48 days with temperatures of 95 degrees and greater. The region has shelters
located in Lancaster at the High Desert MACC and Kensington Campus, with 118 and
111 beds, respectively. In addition, Valley Oasis, the lead CES, provides 63 hotel
vouchers to families. These services provide shelter for 6.2% of the Unhoused in SPA
1. These units are usually full and not available to new individuals in need of shelter until
an individual or family exits. There is a significant number within the City of Palmdale
without the ability to obtain shelter, resulting in a threat to their health and safety. The
County has been working with the City and the nonprofit Advancing Communities
Together to establish a shelter and an emergency bridge housing community to serve
homeless persons in Palmdale.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Resolution No. CC 2024-008 Declaration of Shelter Crisis
January 10, 2024
Page 2

DISCUSSION
On January 10, 2023, the County of Los Angeles declared an emergency, with a revision
on October 3, 2023. The State of California created the California Interagency Council
on Homelessness in 2017 and renamed and restructured the Council in 2021 to develop
policies and identify resources, benefits, and services to prevent and work toward
ending homelessness in California.
A Declaration of Shelter Crisis, under Government Code Section 8698.2 would allow
persons unable to obtain housing to occupy designated public facilities during the
duration of the State of Emergency.

FISCAL IMPACT
$0; The Declaration of Shelter Crisis has no fiscal impact. As needed, when actions are
taken by the City to provide shelter funding will be identified.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal I: Maintain effective public safety and protection for life, property and the
environment.

  catastrophic disasters and emergencies.

BACKGROUND
Project No. 865 includes the removal and replacement of guardrails in two locations. The
existing 350-foot guardrail, located along 25th Street East, north of Spanish Broom Drive,
will be removed and replaced, and the 1,400-foot guardrail, along the west side of Sierra
Highway, will be extended 50 feet north of the existing box culvert. These guardrails have
been damaged and will be replaced with the current standard.

DISCUSSION
On October 09, 2023, the project was advertised electronically through PlanetBids.
The notification was sent to 250 vendors. Twenty-two (22) prospective bidders
downloaded the bid documents.

On October 24, 2023, eight (8) contractors attended the pre-bid meeting.

   City Council Staff Report
DATE:  JANUARY 10, 2024
TO:  HONORABLE MAYOR AND CITY COUNCIL
FROM:  ECONOMIC AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT
DISTRICT:  ALL
SUBJECT:  APPROVE MEMORANDUM OF UNDERSTANDING BY AND
  BETWEEN THE CITY OF PALMDALE AND THE COUNTY OF LOS
  ANGELES TO COLLABORATE ON WATER INFRASTRUCTURE
  PROJECTS LOCATED WITHIN WATERWORKS DISTRICT 40

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council:

  1. Approve Agreement No. A-8677, a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) by and
  between the City of Palmdale (CITY) and the County of Los Angeles (County);
  and,

  2. Authorize the City Manager or their designee to execute the Agreement, including
  minimal and/or non-substantiative changes.

BACKGROUND
Los Angeles County Waterworks District 40 (LACWD) supplies water to approximately
215,000 people throughout the Antelope Valley, including a portion of the City of
Palmdale. The City has been working closely with LACWD to identify necessary
infrastructure projects needed to support residential, commercial and industrial
developments throughout the city. There are approximately 12 million square feet of new
industrial space and over 5,000 new single-family and multifamily residential units in the
development pipeline. Without significant improvements to LACWD’s existing water
infrastructure network, new development projects that will create thousands of new
permanent jobs and temporary construction jobs for the community will not be able to
move forward.

DISCUSSION
The City will enter into an MOU with the County to support the construction of
approximately $23 million dollars worth of infrastructure improvement projects. Projects
include the construction of water wells, pump stations, storage tanks, and water
distribution lines. Without an approved MOU, LACWD will not issue new water Will-
Serve letters to allow development to continue until after needed infrastructure projects
are completed. The planning, design, and permitting for these projects are anticipated
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Agreement No. A-8677
January 10, 2024
Page 2

to take several years to complete. This delay would be detrimental to several time-
sensitive projects, including a new food assembly and distribution center scheduled to
begin construction in a few weeks.

Under the MOU, water infrastructure improvements will be constructed by project
applicants as new projects are approved, or as an alternative, an in-lieu fee will be
collected to fund the improvements. Staff is also working with LACWD to create a
development agreement and reimbursement agreements that will establish a more
detailed project list, phasing plan, and mechanism for developers to potentially recover
a share of the improvement costs as additional development comes on board.

FISCAL IMPACT
None.

STRATEGIC PLAN
Goal III: Invest in infrastructure to improve community livability.

vacancy created by Christian Martinez’s resignation. The recruitment advertisement ran
in the AV Press, the AV Press online, on the Planning Commission webpage, and was
posted on the City’s social media platforms. The City Clerk’s office received three (3)
applications. Attached are the redacted copies of the three (3) applications received by
the City Clerk’s office.

  DISTRICT 5
  Councilmember Alarcón

  Erika Alverdi
  Christina Fraga-Saenz
  Ayeasha Jones

Pursuant to Palmdale Municipal Code Section 2.46.030(B) (2), all such applications shall
be provided to the City Council for review. The Councilmember for the corresponding
district shall, at a regularly scheduled City Council meeting, nominate, from among such
applicants, the person whom the City Councilmember desires to appoint to the Planning
Commission. If the nomination by the Councilmember is approved by a majority vote of
the City Council, the City Councilmember may then proceed to appoint the person to the
Planning Commission.
 Report to Mayor and City Council
Re: Planning Commission Appointment Dist. 5
January 10, 2024
Page 2

If the nomination by the Councilmember is not approved by a majority vote of the City
Council, the City Councilmember will nominate a different candidate until someone is
approved by a majority vote of the City Council.

DISCUSSION
In the recruitment advertisement, the term listed was for the “remainder of a term to expire
in June 2025.”

A Livescan fingerprint submission via the California Department of Justice is required to
complete the appointment. In addition, the State of California requires a Statement of
Economic Interest Form 700 to be filed within 30-days of the appointment.

FISCAL IMPACT
$3,372.12; in advertising costs, budget in Account Number 10112001-722310.
Commissioners also receive compensation of $150 per meeting, a maximum of $300 per
month for the Chair, and $100 per meeting, a maximum of $200 per month for all other
Commissioners budgeted in Account Number 10121001-702.

RECOMMENDATION
Staff recommends that the City Council approve the reappointment of the following
individual as Director and Fifth Public Member to the Palmdale Recycled Water
Authority, for a term to expire January 2025.

  1. Zakeya Anson

BACKGROUND
The Palmdale Recycled Water Authority (“PRWA”) was formed by a Joint Exercise of
Powers (“Agreement”) between the City of Palmdale and the Palmdale Water District
(“PWD”). The purpose of the PRWA is to study, promote, develop, distribute, construct,
install, finance, use and manage recycled water resources.

DISCUSSION
In January 2023, Ms. Zakeya Anson was reappointed by the City Council as the Fifth
Public Member of the PRWA. Ms. Anson has expressed a desire to continue to serve
as Director of the Palmdale Recycled Water Authority. The Palmdale Water District
(“PWD”) Board of Directors will also be seeking reappointment for Ms. Anson at their
January meeting.

Pursuant to Article 4 Organization; Board of Directors, the governing body of the Authority
shall be the Board, which shall consist of five Directors. The governing body of each
Member shall appoint and designate in writing two Directors who shall be authorized to
act for and on behalf of the Member on matters within the powers of the Authority. The
person appointed and designated as Director shall be a member of the Member's
governing body. The fifth Director shall be appointed jointly by both Member Agencies.

  remain in effect, until this Agreement is terminated pursuant to Article 8.

2.2  Formation. There is formed as of the Effective Date a public agency named the
  "Palmdale Recycled Water Authority." Pursuant to Sections 6506 and 6507 of the Act,
  the Authority is an independent public agency separate from the Members. Unless
  otherwise agreed by the Members, the debts, liabilities, and obligations of the Authority
  are not debts, liabilities or obligations of the Members.

  beneficial uses, including irrigation and recharge, and to finance the acquisition and
  construction or installation of recycled water facilities, recharge facilities and irrigation
